newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open higher, Greenspan takes stage.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open higher, Greenspan takes stage.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened modestly higher on Tuesday and were expected to stay in tight ranges ahead of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony later this afternoon.
"It's all up to the chairman today," said one head trader at a U.S. primary dealership. "This should be treated like an FOMC meeting."
In early trading, the 30-year bond was at 101-9/32, up 6/32 from Monday. Its yield edged down to 6.53 percent 6.54 percent.
Traders said they did not expect the early gains to stick, especially with the Treasury slated to sell $15.5 billion in two-year notes just before Greenspan's testimony begins.
Some further concession was anticipated for the notes, currently trading at 5.94 percent on a when-issued basis.

"I think if there weren't an auction the market wold grind higher," said a trader. "But there is no reason to jump in front of a train. People would rather pay (5.90 percent) for them tomorrow than 5.94 today with the risk of them going to 6 percent."

Also this session, the BTM-Schroders weekly chain store sales report will be officially released at 0900 EDT. Rumors circulated in the market that the index fell 0.8 percent in the week ended July 19.
At 1455 EDT, Redbook Research's weekly retail sales data are due.
Traders said reaction should be muted due to Greenspan's speech, which is seen shaping the market's near-term monetary policy expectations.
At February's installment, Greenspan used his testimony to hint at the Fed's rate hike in late March.
The general consensus is that the Fed chief will give a balanced assesment of the economy -- not too sober, not too euphoric.
Market reaction to the testimony depends on which way he tilts, traders said.

Should Greenspan suggest the Fed will keep rates steady for the time being, the market will most likely do much better, players said. But a hint at higher rates at some point could spook the market, although any selling is seen brief.
Ahead of the testimony, investors overseas nibbled at the market during the night in both Tokyo and London, buying mainly in intermediates, traders said.
In early morning trading, the outstanding two-year note was at 100-5/32, up 1/32, to yield 5.91 percent.
Five-year notes were up 2/32 to 100-12/32, yielding 6.16 and 10-year notes were up 3/32 to 102-23/32, yielding 6.25 percent.
